scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes project_change_orders + project_items; project_change_orders + project_links; project_change_orders + project_progress_logs and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

scenarios.oracle: a multi-row or multi-table write either lands whole or not at all; a half-applied write is visible as an inconsistency in the ledger

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes project_change_orders + project_items; project_change_orders + project_links; project_change_orders + project_progress_logs and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

'Load failed: injected server fault' was present at the ~1.3s sample and GONE at ~10s, while three zeros stayed on screen at both, and the 'Live · refreshed on load' provenance chip stayed up throughout - a positive freshne
findings.detail: QUALIFIED, NOT WITHDRAWN - the page does speak, but only for about a second. 'Load failed: injected server fault' was present at the ~1.3s sample and GONE at ~10s, while three zeros stayed on screen at both, and the 'Live · refreshed on load' provenance chip stayed up throughout - a positive freshness claim made while the data is absent. So the row's evidence is real and its third clause - 'without rendering an empty result as though the server had honestly answered none' - holds only for the lifetime of a toast. A reader who arrives three seconds late sees confident zeros with nothing to contradict them. IT ALSO LEAKS THE INJECTION STRING: 'Load failed: injected server fault' is the raw server message concatenated into the notice, so in production this surface shows a person whatever Postgres said. That is the same class as a bare 42501 reaching a signed-in reader. A notice should name what failed and what to do, not echo the backend. FIX (batched per A15): sentinel the figures on error so the STATE carries the failure rather than a transient channel, and render a human sentence instead of the upstream message. || METHOD: WHOLE-SURFACE INJECTION, SAMPLED TWICE. Every /rest/v1/, /functions/v1/ and /rpc/ request is answered 500 {code:500,message:...} with /auth/v1/ deliberately left alive so the identity guard can still read a valid session; interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous; the surface is read at ~1.3s and again ~10s later. THE SECOND SAMPLE IS THE POINT: the failure notice on several of these pages is a toast that auto-dismisses, so a single-instant reading of this oracle is not reproducible - which is why an earlier pass on this bank recorded 'says nothing on failure' across 11 of 16 pages, RETRACTED it as a <main>-scoped lens artefact, and a later pass recorded 12 of 12 passing. Sampling twice shows how both happened. POSITIVE CONTROL, same lens, same run: community's '✕ Could not load posts' and analytics' 'Analysis failed, check console' were caught at BOTH samples, so a silent reading is the page's silence rather than the lens's blindness - the check the retracted finding lacked. Guarded on identity and on pathname, so a session drop or a bounce to the landing page refuses instead of reading a shell.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. findings.detail: THE RETRACTION ON THIS ROW WAS ITSELF WRONG, and this note supersedes it. Three measurements of fail_partial exist and only the middle one is contaminated: (1) FIRST READ, text scope = <main>: failed on 13 of 16 pages. (2) SECOND READ, after I widened the scope to include body-level notice regions: passed on 12 of 12 - and on the strength of that I retracted the finding on 12 pages, writing that 'the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf'. (3) THIRD READ, after I made my own 401 notice CLEAR ITSELF: fails on 9 of 12. NOTHING ON ANY PARTIAL CODE PATH CHANGED ACROSS THOSE THREE. What changed in (2) is that the central session notice I had just added to getDb() was still pinned to the page from the 401 injection earlier in the same failures() run, so namesTheFailure was matching MY OWN leftover text - 'Your session expired, so this page could not be loaded' - rather than anything the page said about a truncated payload. Reading (1) and reading (3) AGREE with each other; (2) is the outlier, and (2) is the one I acted on. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 13 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

findings.detail: MEASURED BY ACTUALLY DOING IT: a project was created through the page's OWN path (saveProject), read back with psql as postgres, and looked for on screen by GEOMETRY - a real box, display not none, visibility not hidden, opacity not zero. NOT BANKED - AND NOT A DEFECT EITHER. THE PROBE ASSERTED FROM THE WRONG FILTER. Immediately after the save the project WAS visible (#d-name, 262x27 - the page navigates to the new project's detail view). After the reload it was absent from the DOM entirely (afterReloadFound: 0) on a page that had genuinely SETTLED at 1,558 characters - so this is not a looked-too-early artifact. ★THE CAUSE IS A DEFAULT MEETING A FILTER, and the page is behaving correctly. projects.status defaults to 'planning' in the schema, and the list the reload lands on was filtered to 'Active 4'. A newly created project is therefore NOT in the Active view - the person clicks a filter and sees it. Recording a red here would accuse the page of hiding work it is correctly filing under a different status, which is the same shape as logbook, where a fresh personal entry legitimately sits behind the Team / My-Entries switch. ★AND THIS RUN ALSO FIXED A THRESHOLD I HAD INVENTED. findings.detail: NOT A DEFECT - THE PAGE IS BEHAVING AS DESIGNED, AND THE CAUSE IS NOW READ FROM THE SOURCE RATHER THAN INFERRED. A project was created through saveProject(), reached `projects` (+1 row), and was visible IMMEDIATELY in the detail view it navigates to (#d-name, 262x27). After a reload it was absent from the DOM entirely, on a page that had genuinely SETTLED (three consecutive equal size readings at 1,558 characters) - so this is not a looked-too-early artifact. ★THE ROOT CAUSE, CORRECTED. My first reading blamed a status FILTER. Reading the code instead: the list query fetches EVERY status (no status predicate at all - only hive_id and deleted_at). The list then GROUPS by status and opens only one group by default: `const open = (_groupOpen[status] !== undefined) ? _groupOpen[status] : (status === 'active')`, with the file's own comment 'auto-expand active, collapse others (user-toggleable)'. projects.status DEFAULTS to 'planning' in the schema. So a newly created project is filed into the PLANNING group, which is COLLAPSED - correctly stored, correctly grouped, one click from view. Recording a red would accuse the page of hiding work it is deliberately organising. ★AND THIS IS A PROBE THAT IS NOT FINISHED, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT STATEMENT FROM A PAGE THAT IS BROKEN. The instrument now expands what it can find (details[not open], aria-expanded=false, generic group-header classes - 3 elements expanded this run) but still does not reach THIS page's group headers, so the planning group stays shut and the row stays unrendered. That is my selector not matching, not the product failing. ★THREE INVENTED CONSTANTS HAVE NOW BEEN REPLACED BY PROPERTIES IN THIS ONE ORACLE, each after being wrong: a text scan became element GEOMETRY (innerText on a hidden element falls back to textContent); a name-based blocklist of toast-like hosts became RELOAD-SURVIVAL (an echo cannot survive a refresh, a record must); and a 2,500-character readiness floor became SETTLE-DETECTION (project-manager legitimately settles at 1,558, so that floor could only ever time out here). findings.title: MEASURED AND FAILING - 13 of 13 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: wizardSubmit, saveProject (listener-bound), deleteProject, cycleScopeStatus, linkSuggested, saveLink, removeLink, ackLog ….
findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - 13 of 13 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: wizardSubmit, saveProject (listener-bound), deleteProject, cycleScopeStatus, linkSuggested, saveLink, removeLink, ackLog …. THE PREMISE WAS CHECKED FIRST, because filing this against a page that is guarded elsewhere would be a manufactured finding: utils.js already defines whRequireOnline(action, notify) and exposes it as window.whRequireOnline, and it already carries the exact sentence this oracle asks for - 'You are offline. <action> needs a connection - nothing was sent, so nothing is half-done.' The scanner's GUARD pattern matches RequireOnline( and navigator.onLine === false, so a page that called either would have counted as guarded. None of these writes call anything. This is NON-ADOPTION of a centralized, correctly-worded helper, not a missing message. WHY THE PLATFORM'S EXISTING GREEN DOES NOT COVER THIS: tools/validate_offline_write_guard.py PASSES at fail-severity, but its PAGES list is exactly ['marketplace.html', 'marketplace-seller.html'] - 19 writes on two pages. None of the 22 roster pages is in its scope, so its green says nothing about them. And widening that list alone would NOT be enough: the validator's user_invokable() recognises only window.X = and inline onclick/onchange/onsubmit, so of the 53 exposed writes measured across the roster it would see 37 and miss the 16 bound with addEventListener. WHAT A PASSIVE BANNER DOES NOT DO, since every page already adopts one: the banner states the condition, it does not refuse the action. The button still fires, the request still leaves, and the person still cannot tell whether their work landed - which is the whole distinction this oracle draws. THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER WRITE at the top of each function - if (!whRequireOnline('<gerund>', showToast)) return; - and the highest-stakes ones on this page should go first. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS after the guards land: prove it LIVE rather than statically, and note that setOffline does not flip navigator.onLine in the page, so the probe must override navigator.onLine AND block the network, then assert that zero requests fired and the sentence reached the person.

findings.detail: THE GUARD IS IN PLACE AND ITS MECHANISM IS LIVE-PROVEN ELSEWHERE - what is missing is a live walk of THIS page's control, and R6 bars a structural check from settling a behavioural oracle, so this stays owed rather than being banked on the guard's presence. tools/prove_offline_refusal.mjs currently proves the same helper on 8 controls across 7 pages (skillmatrix exam, report-sender send + contact, community reaction, alert-hub dismiss, shift-brain publish, index persona, inventory part-delete), covering every notify channel variant the platform uses - a page toast, a create-on-demand toast, #sheet-error, #email-error, #wh-toast and showAmcMsg. GUARDED THIS SESSION on this page - fourteen writes, the largest adoption of any surface, because this is the financial page and it registers a queue for only ONE of its tables: approveCO, rejectCO, saveRole, removeRole, wizardSubmit, saveProject, deleteProject, cycleScopeStatus, linkSuggested, saveLink, removeLink, ackLog, cancelCO, saveLessons. The approval and role writes were placed BEFORE their confirmation dialogs on purpose: making a supervisor commit to 'cost / schedule impact will be reflected in the project' and only then failing leaves them unable to tell whether it was recorded. Both change-order paths carry an optimistic lock (.eq('status','pending')) so a concurrent decision cannot be reversed - and a lock that never reaches the database protects nothing, which is precisely why refusing beats firing here. NOTE ON THE PAGE'S QUEUE: window._whPmProgressQueue covers project_progress_logs only. ackLog writes that table, so it was checked for a queue path INSIDE the function - there is none, so it was firing into a dead network and is correctly refused. WHY THE LIVE WALK DID NOT LAND: the create-project wizard never exposed #wiz-create at non-zero width from the list view within 22 attempts - it is a multi-step wizard, so the reach has to advance the steps rather than fill every visible field and press Create. findings.detail: FAILS: with 2 reads answered 500, **no retry control is present** - zero visible elements whose label mentions retry or try-again. Its three project heroes also read 0 with no explanation, so the reader has neither a diagnosis nor a control. SO THE ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant costs the whole page again on the connection that just failed. THE PATTERN EXISTS ON THIS PLATFORM, so this is adoption: achievements renders a Retry button beside its toast, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 post cards. Only 2 of 22 pages have one. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that RE-ISSUES the failed read - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**. Only 2 offer a retry CONTROL (achievements, community); public-feed's was measured firing a real re-request and rendering 15 posts.

findings.detail:
MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. RETRY PATH - FAILS, and the half that is certain is the half that matters. Under an injected 500 this page offers ZERO retry affordances: no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'refresh' control. That is confirmed TWO independent ways - the lens counted affordances:0, and a separate direct probe that 500'd every /rest/v1/ request and scanned the whole document for a retry control also found none. A person whose data failed to load has nothing to press. ★ONE HALF OF THIS VERDICT IS INSTRUMENT-DEPENDENT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN BANKED AS FACT: the lens also reported saysFailure:False. My direct probe, which failed EVERY read rather than the subset the lens induces, and which scanned the whole page rather than <main>, found that this page DOES say something failed under a total outage. So the page's failure MESSAGING may be better than the lens's number suggests - a partial induction can leave a surface half-populated and quiet. The missing retry CONTROL is not in doubt; the missing failure SENTENCE is, on this page. WHY IT IS NOT BANKED GREEN ANYWAY: the oracle asks for a retry PATH, and a failure a person cannot act on is the shape this family exists to catch - 'a failure that offers a retry which does not re-attempt is worse than one that offers none', and offering none at all is the floor of that same scale.

Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.

findings.detail: FAILS: the detail read was answered 500 and the page correctly said 'Could not load project', but **no retry control accompanies it** - the only affordance is re-clicking the card, which is not presented as a retry and gives no signal that it would re-attempt. CREDIT WHERE DUE, AND THE GAP IS NARROW: because `#list-view` stays on screen, this page's reader is not stranded the way a blank detail would strand them - the failure costs a click rather than a reload. That makes the missing control a smaller defect here than on the surfaces that go blank, and it is still the difference between 'the app offered to fix it' and 'the reader guessed'. MEASURED ON THE V2 VIEW ITSELF, WITH THE INJECTION ARMED AFTER INITIAL LOAD. This is the technique the slow_honest repair established: a modal, tab or detail view cannot be reached while the read that renders its opener is still failing, so the `window.fetch` wrapper starts INERT, the page is allowed to load normally, the fail flag is then set, and the view is opened - so the request answered 500 is the VIEW'S OWN. Exactly 1 read was intercepted in each case, which is the count the view fires. THIS MATTERS BECAUSE THE ALTERNATIVE PRODUCED FOURTEEN UNSOUND ROWS. Filtering rows by oracle name alone and applying one page-load reading to both view subjects banked V2 evidence describing a view never visited - a claim resting on something other than what it names (R7). Verdicts here are scoped to the view in this row's own `subject`.

evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow IN THIS VIEW - it never answers with a server-derived value it does not have yet
evidence.checked: WHY THIS ROW WAS RE-MEASURED. Its previous evidence was IDENTICAL to the V1 row's on the same page - a KPI-tile reading taken at page load - because the banking loop selected rows by oracle name and swept both views with one page-level measurement. Fourteen V2 rows across the platform carried a measurement of a view they never visited, which is R7's exact failure: a claim resting on something other than what it names. The count did not move; the evidence did. PASSES, AND THE MECHANISM IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE I FIRST READ IT AS A DEFECT. Arming the delay and clicking a project card fired `projects?id=eq.170cf794-a67d-4791-afdc-cffc95042cac` with 0 resolved, and a body-wide keyword sweep matched 'No projects' - which looked like an emptiness claim during load. Scoping it properly refuted that: **`#list-view` was still shown (h=1187) and `#detail-view` was hidden (h=0)**, and the matched text was the LOADED list's own legitimate copy - `pm-card-blocked` reading 'On hold or planning 0 - No projects waiting to start or on hold' against a true zero, beside 'Active projects 4' and 'Past end date 3'. SO THE REAL BEHAVIOUR IS THE GOOD ONE: this page keeps the list on screen and swaps to the detail only once the data lands - it never paints a blank detail. After the read resolved, the detail rendered 'WO-2026-001 Recurring Compressor Breakdown Bundle'. RECORDED AGAINST ANOTHER ORACLE, NOT THIS ONE: during the ~9s wait there is no progress indicator at all, so the click appears to do nothing. That is a what_happens_next gap, not a fabrication. MEASURED WITH THE DELAY ARMED AFTER INITIAL LOAD, which is what makes a V2 view measurable at all. A modal or thread cannot be opened while the feed that renders its opener is still pending, so the fetch wrapper starts INERT and is armed only once the page has settled; the view is then opened and its OWN read is the one held in flight. Every reading below is refused unless `resolved === 0` at measurement time and at least one request was intercepted, so neither a vacuous run nor an already-resolved one can be reported as a pass. AND WHERE NUMERIC WRITES ARE COUNTED, THEY ARE ATTRIBUTED BY CONTAINMENT: each write's ancestor chain is walked and only writes landing INSIDE this view's container count, so a page-level write cannot credit or convict the wrong view. evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: member (role floor on budget) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); engineering_calcs (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / m
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); engineering_calcs (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); pm_completions (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 16 read relation(s), 10 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, engineering_calcs, hive_members, pm_completions, project_change_orders, project_items, project_links, proje).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); engineering_calcs (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / m
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); engineering_calcs (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); pm_completions (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 16 read relation(s), 10 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, engineering_calcs, hive_members, pm_completions, project_change_orders, project_items, project_links, proje).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

scenarios.oracle: progress % states its basis - weighted by cost, item count, or planned hours; a bare % is a claim nobody can check

evidence.asserts: FIXED a caption that implied the wrong basis. The percentage is an hours-WEIGHTED average of each item's own pct_complete - weight = estimated_hours, defaulting to 1 - and the same formula is implemented twice and agrees: in python-api/projects/descriptive.py ('Weighted percent complete (by estimated_hours)') which the edge function serves, and in the client-side rollup that runs when that service is unavailable. But the caption beneath the figure read only 'N/M items done', a DIFFERENT statistic, so a reader naturally took the percentage for the item ratio. Two items at 50% weigh very differently when one is a 2-hour task and the other a 200-hour overhaul. The caption now names the basis, and names the FALLBACK honestly rather than always claiming hours: with no estimated hours on any item the weights collapse to 1 and it really is an equal-weight average, which is what it now says.
evidence.checked: The basis was traced to the code that actually computes what this KPI displays, not to the first plausible rollup: the detail figure comes from _progress.rollup - the project-progress edge function's payload, backed by the Python module - NOT from the client list rollup I read first. That distinction caught a real defect in my own fix: my initial caption read a field I had set on the LIST projects (_pct_basis), which is undefined on the edge-fn rollup, so it would have printed 'weighted by planned hours' unconditionally - a label that is right by accident and wrong whenever hours are absent. It now derives from hours_estimated, which the payload already carries, and both branches were exercised.
evidence.value_checked: python descriptive.py: total_w = sum(estimated_hours or 1); weighted_pct = sum(pct_complete * (estimated_hours or 1)) | client fallback: identical formula | caption with hours (hours_estimated=120): 'weighted by planned hours · 3/10 items done' | without (hours_estimated=0): 'equal weight per item · 3/10 items done' | field absent: 'equal weight per item'

subject.name: budget carries currency and VAT treatment

scenarios.oracle: budget figures carry their currency and whether they include VAT

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK. The oracle wants a budget figure to carry its currency AND its VAT treatment. Currency was already explicit (the field reads 'Budget (PHP)' and every figure renders through fmtPHP as whole-peso en-PH). VAT was never mentioned anywhere on the page, and the earlier search that appeared to find it was matching the letters v-a-t inside reservation, elevator and activated. I did NOT invent a tax policy, because which basis a plant tracks is a business fact I cannot read off the code. What IS readable, and is what a reader actually needs, is the SYSTEM's behaviour: WorkHive applies no VAT logic anywhere - a platform-wide search for vat_rate, vat_inclusive, value-added-tax and any tax column returns nothing outside unrelated 12% matches (NaOCl concentration, lift handling capacity, a DOE cost-savings figure, a CSS tint). So the figure is stored exactly as typed. That is now stated in all three places a budget is touched: both entry fields say the figure is stored as entered with no VAT adjustment and to use the basis finance tracks, and the 'Budget at completion' KPI - which had no sub-caption while its sibling 'Actual cost' already carried 'proxy: hours x P200' - now reads 'PHP, as entered (no VAT adjustment applied)'. A silent ambiguity becomes a stated one, which is the same shape as every other -_stated oracle on this bank.
evidence.checked: Enumerated the VAT surface before claiming absence rather than after: a repo-wide regex over html/js/ts/sql for VAT, vat_rate, vat_inclusive, value-added-tax and 12% returned zero tax handling, so 'no VAT adjustment' is a measured property of the code, not an assumption. Located every budget touchpoint instead of only the one the oracle named - two entry fields (wizard and edit modal) plus the BAC KPI - because stating it only at entry leaves the reader of the figure uninformed, which is where this class of defect survives. Each edit asserted a unique anchor match before replacing, and the KPI edit sits inside a JS template literal, so it was re-verified afterwards: ${fmtPHP(ev.bac)} intact and 0 backticks introduced.

evidence.asserts: Three distinct money figures, each labelled with its full name AND its standard abbreviation, and none standing in for another: 'Budget at completion', 'Planned value (PV)', 'Earned value (EV)', 'Actual cost (AC)'. They are separate fields in the payload too (bac/pv/ev/ac from the EVM computation), not one number re-rendered under three captions. The derived figures show their arithmetic rather than asserting it - 'Schedule variance (SV = EV - PV)' and 'Cost variance (CV = EV - AC)' carry the formula in the label - so a reader can reconstruct them. THE BEST DETAIL IS THE HONESTY ON AC: it is captioned 'proxy: hours x P200'. Actual cost here is DERIVED from logged hours, not invoiced spend, and saying so directly under the number is what stops the exact substitution this oracle guards against - a labour proxy read as real money committed. TERMINOLOGY NOTED, not glossed: the triad implemented is the EVM standard one (planned / earned / actual), not planned / COMMITTED / actual. Committed cost - obligated but not yet paid - is not tracked anywhere on this page. The substantive requirement is met; the third concept is a different one.
evidence.checked: Traced from the computation to the caption rather than reading either alone: diagnostic.py returns bac/pv/ev/ac/sv/cv/spi/cpi as separate rounded values, and each renders in its own KPI cell through fmtPHP (which delegates to the shared whFmtPeso and yields '-' rather than a NaN peso sign for a null). findings.title: selector pointed at the container, not this subject
findings.detail: WITHDRAWN BY ME, same turn, before anyone relied on it. I banked this from page_component_selectors.json, and an audit of that map against the bank's own subject NAMES found this entry points at the wrong element: the subject is a ROW/CARD and my selector was its CONTAINER (or a generic utility class like .btn/.ic/.card that matches unrelated furniture). Measuring a container and recording it against a row subject is exactly the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this scoped prover was built to END - I reintroduced it one level up, in the map rather than the reading. The reading itself was real; it was just a reading of something else. Returned to owed pending a corrected selector.

findings.title: FAILS: with 10 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 1532 characters before the refusal and 813 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than I
findings.detail: FAILS: with 10 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 1532 characters before the refusal and 813 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than IDENTITY, because this platform has already shipped that exact inversion - a 42501 rendered as 'your session has expired', which sends a signed-IN person to re-authenticate for a problem authentication cannot fix, and 401/403 collapsed into one message so neither audience got a true statement. ZERO of the 16 graded pages made that mistake on this run. utils.js:1607 whIsAuthFailure() is why: it returns FALSE for status 403 with the comment 'authenticated, and refused. Not a session problem', and documents 42501 as insufficient_privilege. That discrimination is holding. HOW THE REFUSAL WAS INDUCED, and why it is the real branch: every Supabase REST read is answered with the body PostgREST actually sends for a row-level-security refusal - HTTP 403 with {"code":"42501","message":"permission denied for table"} - so the page's own error handling takes the same path it would in production. The patch is on window.fetch, NOT page.route, because a warm service worker serves from cache and bypasses route interception; it is installed with addInitScript in a context closed after each page so it cannot leak. NON-WRITING: it makes a READ return 403. THE INJECTION PROVES ITSELF: every intercepted call increments a counter, and a page where the counter is zero is UNGRADED rather than judged. That guard exists because the first version of this prover silently did nothing - a regex written inside a template literal collapsed to one that terminates at its second character, so the init script was a SyntaxError, every read succeeded normally, and the prover reported 'the reads were all refused and the page said nothing' while nothing had been refused at all. Hit counts on this run ranged from 8 to 42 per page. AND THE SIGNAL MUST APPEAR: the same page is read WITHOUT the injection first, and if its ordinary copy already matches the refusal vocabulary the page is UNGRADED - which is exactly what happened to skillmatrix, whose normal text contains a matching phrase. Without that control a page whose everyday copy happens to say 'cannot' would pass for free. THE SYNTHESIS - THIS IS ONE MISSING SURFACE, NOT 15 PAGE BUGS. Of 16 graded pages: 13 said NOTHING AT ALL when every read was refused, 2 showed only a GENERIC error ('Analysis failed, check console'; 'Achievements failed to load.'), and 1 passed. The platform already has the pieces - a central WRITE-failure message and the correct 401-vs-403 discriminator in utils.js - but there is no equivalent on the READ path, so a refused read renders as dashes or blanks with no explanation. On logbook the numbers '516 entries 30 machines 6 open' became '- entries - machines - open' with the body text identical to the character (1107 before and after) and not one word about why. A person cannot tell 'there is no data' from 'the load failed' from 'you are not allowed', and those three call for three different actions. THE FIX IS ONE ADOPTION, not 15 edits: give the read path the same treatment the write path already has. This independently reproduces a finding already recorded as 'the message already exists; the gap is ADOPTION on the read path'. SCOPE: V1, the page as it loads, and READ refusal only - a refused WRITE is a different path with its own central message, and is not claimed here. 5 of the 22 pages are excluded from the sweep because they are public or have no authenticated read to refuse. The walk is NON-WRITING.

findings.title: submit control sits behind a form the probe did not fill
findings.detail:
MEASURED, NOT BANKED - kept so the next session does not re-derive it. tools/prove_double_fire.mjs reached this page with all writes intercepted and held (nothing could be written), but pressing "Complete
0" produced no mutating request — it opens a view or validates a form rather than submitting, so this oracle has no subject here The submit control on this page lives BEHIND a form or modal that must be opened AND filled before it will attempt a write, so a top-level press only opens a view. UNGRADED rather than failed: reporting "no double-fire guard" about a control that never submits anything is a fabricated defect. TO CLOSE THIS ROW the harness needs a per-page flow that opens the form, fills the minimum valid fields, and THEN double-presses - with the same write interception, which is what makes doing so safe.

evidence.asserts: this view has no committing control, so there is no second press that could write twice
evidence.checked: NOT APPLICABLE: the project list has no action to press twice - a filter applied twice is still one filter. My verb-matching heuristic flagged it only because its label happens to start with the word 'Complete' - a reminder that a control's LABEL is not its function, which is why this row names what the element actually is. Shared chrome (nav hub search, page-guide chip, companion launcher, feedback FAB, session and search overlays) is excluded by name, since counting the nav search field would make all 22 pages look like forms. This page's committing actions are raised in their own dialogs - the change order on V3, the budget sheet - and are graded there. Recorded declared-na rather than green (a pass over an empty denominator, which R10 forbids) or failed (which would invent an action). SCOPED TO THIS VIEW, not the page - the distinction that had 32 rows re-homed when modal readings turned out to be filed against a list view. EXPIRES if this view ever gains a committing control.
